messages.subject: I can't set up Stan, some problem with Xcode??
parts:
Hi, I'm trying to set up Stan on a borrowed Mac. I just installed R and
Rstudio so these are the latest versions (Rstudio 0.98.484, R 3.0.2). I
installed Xcode as instructed, then I went into Xcode and installed
Command Line Tools. I installed inline and Rcpp in R. I even followed
the "Special Steps for Xcode 5.0.1 + R 3.0.2 + Mac OS X 10.9 (Mavericks)".
I have no idea if that applies to me, but I thought it would be worth a
try. To create and edit this file, I had to go back to my Unix knowledge
and use vi.

Then, to be on the safe side, I then quit Rstudio, quit Xcode, and
restarted Rstudio. Then I tried the hello world code in R and it didn't
work (see below). So now I don't know what to do!
A

P.S. Just one minor thing on that help page. The RStudio section (under
the Prerequisites section) is confusing. It says, "the safe way is to
execute Sys.getenv('R_ARCH') and see if the result is not empty". But
it's not clear what this means. I think it means that if the result is
empty, there's no need to worry. But it does not say so. Similarly, at
the end of that section, it says, "If you are unsure whether to use the
32-bit or 64-bit configuration, execute the following in R:
> .Platform$r_arch"
Again, I think that if the result is an empty string, there's no need to
worry. But it does not say that. It just says if you're unsure to run
this code, but with no instructions on what to do when the output comes!

OK, now back to my problem:

R transcript below:

---

> library(inline)
> library(Rcpp)

Attaching package: �Rcpp�

The following object is masked from �package:inline�:

registerPlugin

> src <- '
+ std::vector<std::string> s;
+ s.push_back("hello");
+ s.push_back("world");
+ return Rcpp::wrap(s);
+ '
> hellofun <- cxxfunction(body = src, includes = '', plugin = 'Rcpp',
verbose = FALSE)
/bin/sh: llvm-g++-4.2: command not found

Andrew,

Not sure if the last couple of lines got abbreviated, but they should be something like shown below. 

Regards,
Rob J. Goedman
goe...@icloud.com


So for example you could select clang for both C and C++ with extensive checking by having in~/.R/Makevars

CC=clang
CXX=clang++
CFLAGS=-mtune=native -g -O2 -Wall -pedantic -Wconversion
CXXFLAGS=-mtune=native -g -O2 -Wall -pedantic -Wconversion

(the first two are necessary if Xcode 5 was installed and Xcode 4.6 was not previously installed) and for another version of gfortran-4.2 we needed

FLIBS=-lgfortran

On 12/12/13, 1:02 PM, gel...@stat.columbia.edu wrote:
> J
> Thanks for the advice, but I don't understand what to do.

> It looks like
> the file is there, so I don't know what to modify.
> See below for transcript from my terminal.

You're even more literal than me!

Are you trying to follow the instructions in:

https://github.com/stan-dev/rstan/wiki/RStan-Getting-Started

If not, I'd say try that first, then help us make them better
where they're not clear.

There is a section:
Special Steps for Xcode 5.0.1 + R 3.0.2 + Mac OS X 10.9 (Mavericks)

which says:

you need to create a file

~/.R/Makevars

with content

CXX=g++ -arch x86_64 -ftemplate-depth-256 -stdlib=libstdc++
CXXFLAGS="-mtune=native -O3 -Wall -pedantic -Wconversion"

I just modified it to read:

You need to create or edit the file

~/.R/Makevars

so that its content is exactly

CXX=g++ -arch x86_64 -ftemplate-depth-256 -stdlib=libstdc++
CXXFLAGS="-mtune=native -O3 -Wall -pedantic -Wconversion"

I hope that helps.

If other things are unclear in the install instructions, please let
us know and we can try to reword them.

- Bob

parts:
On 12/12/13, 2:25 PM, gel...@stat.columbia.edu wrote:
> The difficulty isn't just the cutting-and-pasting, it's also that a new
> file needs to be created, and that it is being put in a weird place. For
> example, if there were a file to save, and I clicked on it in the Mac, I'd
> have no way to navigate to ~/.R/

My understanding is that given the way R does builds from source,
there's no way to get around this configuration step. Something needs
to put that text in that file.

You can copy it into the right place from the terminal using "cp" or
move it there using "mv". You can create the file in R and save it
into that directory (maybe easiest for an R user? Do you know how to
do that in R?). Or we could provide a file and you could save it.
But then you need to know how to save in your browser on your operating
system.

The "~/" is a unix shorthand for your home directory. For me, it's
a synonym for "/Users/carp". In Safari (the Mac built-in web browser),
you select menu option "File >> Save as...", and it pops up a little
dialog box and under the heading "FAVORITES", I see "carp", which is
my home directory. Now the problem. Because R chose to use ".R" (as
is popular for config), it doesn't get listed by default when you click
on your home directory. But, if you type "~" into the "Export as" box,
it will pop up another dialog box that will let you type the full
path to the file in, here "~/.R/", and hit return, it will go to .R and
list the contents. Then you can add Makevars.

It's hard to know where to stop our instructions in terms of how to
interact with browsers and operating systems. We assumed people knew
how to create and store files, but it looks like we assumed too much
given the tricky nature of this file.

I'm worried about just piling in instructions. Then people don't read
them. You'll note that the last comment from Shravan on your blog
was asking for simpler instructions --- that's because he knew how to
do all the little things we were trying to explain.

We drew the line at telling users how to make a file and
put it in a directory, but perhaps we should keep on going down and give
people a bit more tutorial on using Safari and the Mac OS? The
issue is that then the instructions get huge. Or maybe we have a
"help on this step" button that pulls out more information?

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] I can't set up Stan, some problem with Xcode??
parts:
Hi, Bob. I don't think that we need to tell users how to save a file into a directory. After all, I was able to do it, it just wasn't so easy. But I think the following instructions would be easier (see below). Perhaps Jiqiang can take a look and make sure the command is bulletproof.
A

---

From the R console:

> if (!file.exists ("~/.R/Makevars")) cat ('CXX=g++ -arch x86_64 -ftemplate-depth-256 -stdlib=libstdc++\nCXXFLAGS="-mtune=native -O3 -Wall -pedantic -Wconversion"\n', file="~/.R/Makevars")


---

On Dec 12, 2013, at 9:33 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

>
>

> On 12/12/13, 2:25 PM, gel...@stat.columbia.edu wrote:
>> The difficulty isn't just the cutting-and-pasting, it's also that a new
>> file needs to be created, and that it is being put in a weird place. For
>> example, if there were a file to save, and I clicked on it in the Mac, I'd
>> have no way to navigate to ~/.R/
>
> My understanding is that given the way R does builds from source,
> there's no way to get around this configuration step. Something needs
> to put that text in that file.
>
> You can copy it into the right place from the terminal using "cp" or
> move it there using "mv". You can create the file in R and save it
> into that directory (maybe easiest for an R user? Do you know how to
> do that in R?). Or we could provide a file and you could save it.
> But then you need to know how to save in your browser on your operating
> system.
>
> The "~/" is a unix shorthand for your home directory. For me, it's
> a synonym for "/Users/carp". In Safari (the Mac built-in web browser),
> you select menu option "File >> Save as...", and it pops up a little
> dialog box and under the heading "FAVORITES", I see "carp", which is
> my home directory. Now the problem. Because R chose to use ".R" (as
> is popular for config), it doesn't get listed by default when you click
> on your home directory. But, if you type "~" into the "Export as" box,
> it will pop up another dialog box that will let you type the full
> path to the file in, here "~/.R/", and hit return, it will go to .R and
> list the contents. Then you can add Makevars.
>
> It's hard to know where to stop our instructions in terms of how to
> interact with browsers and operating systems. We assumed people knew
> how to create and store files, but it looks like we assumed too much
> given the tricky nature of this file.
>
> I'm worried about just piling in instructions. Then people don't read
> them. You'll note that the last comment from Shravan on your blog
> was asking for simpler instructions --- that's because he knew how to
> do all the little things we were trying to explain.
>
> We drew the line at telling users how to make a file and
> put it in a directory, but perhaps we should keep on going down and give
> people a bit more tutorial on using Safari and the Mac OS? The
> issue is that then the instructions get huge. Or maybe we have a
> "help on this step" button that pulls out more information?
>
> - Bob
>
>
>>
>> Ideally we could have some code to cut and paste directly into the R
>> console that would write the file. Would that be possible? Other parts
>> of the Stan instructions involving cutting and pasting into the R console,
>> and that seems to work well.
>>
>> A
>>
>>>
>>>

>>>

messages.author: ab7b24da45678eac
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] I can't set up Stan, some problem with Xcode??
parts:
On Thu, Dec 12, 2013 at 3:48 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
Hi, Bob.  I don't think that we need to tell users how to save a file into a directory.  After all, I was able to do it, it just wasn't so easy.   But I think the following instructions would be easier (see below).  Perhaps Jiqiang can take a look and make sure the command is bulletproof.
A

---

From the R console:

> if (!file.exists ("~/.R/Makevars")) cat ('CXX=g++ -arch x86_64 -ftemplate-depth-256 -stdlib=libstdc++\nCXXFLAGS="-mtune=native  -O3 -Wall -pedantic -Wconversion"\n', file="~/.R/Makevars")

It is a good idea.  The issue is that a user might have a file already there, so it is not bulletproof.  The file already there might have the correct configuration or not.  So we need to deal with that differently.  My opinion is to leave it almost as what it is now.  If a user does not know how to do it, it should not be hard to find someone who can help with it. 

--
Jiqiang

P.S.  Just one minor thing on that help page.  The RStudio section (under
the Prerequisites section) is confusing.  It says, "the safe way is to
execute Sys.getenv('R_ARCH') and see if the result is not empty".  But
it's not clear what this means.  I think it means that if the result is
empty, there's no need to worry.  But it does not say so.  Similarly, at
the end of that section, it says, "If you are unsure whether to use the
32-bit or 64-bit configuration, execute the following in R:
.Platform$r_arch"
Again, I think that if the result is an empty string, there's no need to
worry.  But it does not say that.  It just says if you're unsure to run
this code, but with no instructions on what to do when the output comes!

Thanks, Andrew --- should've read this message first and it
would've answered my first question!

Jiqiang -- can you clarify the instructions?  I'm not sure
what the answer is or I'd do it myself.
- Bob
